lesson.title: Where the Signal Comes Out: The Op-Amp Output
lesson.summary: The op-amp output is a single, low-impedance terminal whose voltage equals the open-loop gain times the difference between the two inputs, but it can never exceed the supply rails, so a large enough input difference simply drives it into saturation.
lesson.body:
Every path traced through the inverting and non-inverting inputs eventually arrives at the same single terminal at the point of the op-amp symbol's triangle: the output. Unlike the two inputs, which form a differential pair measuring a voltage difference, the output is single-ended, meaning its voltage is measured relative to the circuit's common ground reference, not relative to some other floating terminal.

Two properties define an ideal op-amp output. First, its output impedance is zero, meaning it can supply whatever current a load demands without its voltage sagging, a stark contrast to the near-infinite impedance of the two input terminals. Real op-amps only approximate this, with open-loop output impedances typically in the tens to low hundreds of ohms, and with hard limits on how much current they can actually source or sink before the output voltage collapses or the device current-limits itself. Second, and just as important, the output voltage can never exceed the power supply rails feeding the op-amp, and in practice falls a volt or two short of each rail even at its extreme, an effect often called headroom loss (some newer parts, marketed as rail-to-rail output devices, get much closer to the actual supply voltages).

That rail limit interacts directly with the huge open-loop gain from the previous two chapters, and a worked example shows exactly how. Take an op-amp with Aol = 200,000, powered from +/-15 V supplies, and apply a differential input of 200 microvolts, V+ minus V- equal to 0.0002 V. The ideal, unclamped output would be Vout = 200,000 x 0.0002 = 40 V. But the supply can only provide up to about +15 V, so the real output does not reach 40 V at all, it saturates, pinned at roughly the positive rail (in practice a volt or so below +15 V once headroom is accounted for, so perhaps around +13 to +14 V for a typical device). Any further increase in the input difference changes nothing further at the output; it is already as high as the supply will allow.

This saturation behavior is the single biggest reason open-loop op-amp operation is rarely useful for linear amplification: since it takes only a few hundred microvolts of input difference to slam the output into one rail or the other, an op-amp run without feedback behaves almost like a switch, fully positive or fully negative, with essentially no useful territory in between. That switch-like behavior is not wasted, though, it becomes exactly the desired behavior for a comparator once positive feedback is added, covered later in this chapter. But for the op-amp to behave as a well-controlled, proportional amplifier, something has to rein in that enormous open-loop gain before the output has any chance to saturate on a small, legitimate input signal, which is the entire purpose of the negative feedback covered next.
